newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia says Chechnya had no right to expel OSCE man.
newsitem.headline: Russia says Chechnya had no right to expel OSCE man.

text.p: Russia on Wednesday condemned a decision by Chechnya to expel the OSCE's head of mission but the move appeared to reflect divisions among leaders of the rebel region rather than any toughening of their approach to Moscow.

Deputy Foreign Minister Boris Kolokolov, speaking a day after the abrupt expulsion of Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) mission chief Tim Guldimann, said only Moscow had the right to take such a step.
"Chechnya is part of the Russian Federation and has no right to make anyone persona non grata," he told Interfax news agency.

The incident and the reactions it provoked in Chechnya suggested passions were running high between the outgoing administration of Zemlikhan Yandarbiyev and President-elect Aslan Maskhadov, whose victory at last week's poll has been welcomed by the Kremlin.
Maskhadov, who won if not Moscow's confidence then at least its ear during peace talks last year, is due to be sworn into office on February 12.

Yandarbiyev's "foreign ministry", not recognised as such by Moscow, ordered Swiss diplomat Guldimann out of the region on Tuesday, criticising him for referring to Chechnya as a part of the Russian Federation.
But Ruslan Kutayev, head of the main party which supported Maskhadov, said the outgoing cabinet did not have the right to expel the respected Swiss diplomat.

"It is a private opinion of a person who does not represent the official position of Grozny any more," Interfax quoted Kutayev as saying. Maskhadov's team said the OSCE had fulfilled its role in overseeing elections in a proper manner.
Guldimann played an important role in organising talks between Moscow and Chechen separatists during the 21-month conflict in which tens of thousands of people were killed.
Russian conservatives have repeatedly demanded his expulsion, accusing him of being biased in the rebels' favour.
On Wednesday, Guldimann was in Nazran, the capital of the neighbouring ethnic republic of Ingushetia. He has so far refused to comment, but has held talks with Ingush President Ruslan Aushev.
"(He) is waiting it out for the next few days to see what happens. He expects that when the new government takes office this will be reversed," an OSCE spokeswoman in Vienna said on Tuesday.

Under a peace agreement between Moscow and the separatists, Russia withdrew its remaining forces from Chechnya last month, marking the end of an abortive military campaign launched in 1994 to crush a Chechen drive for independence.
The agreement deferred a final decision on Chechnya's future status until the year 2001, though both sides are engaged in a war of words over the issue.
Both Yandarbiyev and Maskhadov say Chechnya is independent already while Moscow offers only a high degree of autonomy within the Russian Federation.
All leading presidential candidates vowed to maintain unity and avoid feuding, but the move against Guildimann appeared to be a bitter parting shot from Yandarbiyev.
Russia, sensitive to any suggestion of recognition by a foreign power, warned foreign officials not to accept invitations to Maskhadov's inauguration without consulting Moscow.
"Any official action on Chechnya by foreign states bypassing federal authorities would be considered as unfriendly action," Foreign Ministry spokesman Mikhail Demurin told Itar-Tass news agency.
